newsitem.title: INDIA: India, U.S. to sign extradition treaty.
newsitem.headline: India, U.S. to sign extradition treaty.

text.p: India and the United States will sign an extradition treaty next week during a visit by a senior Indian official aimed at strengthening ties between the two biggest democracies, the Foreign Ministry said on Friday.

Indian junior Foreign Minister Saleem Iqbal Shervani and Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott are due on June 25 to sign an extradition treaty that will underscore the two nations' determination to combat terrorism, a ministry spokesman said.
"This will be the first high-level contact between our government and the new team in the U.S. administration," the spokesman told Reuters.
Shervani, who is already in the United States on personal business, is scheduled to start his four-day official visit to Washington and Chicago on June 23.

Shervani, who was named to his post last week, will also meet President Bill Clinton's newly appointed Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Thomas Pickering and Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade Stuart Eizenstat.

Foreign Ministry officials said the speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives, Newt Gingrich, was likely to visit India in August to participate in celebrations of India's 50th anniversary of independence from British colonial rule.

The Press Trust of India quoted a Foreign Ministry official as saying Clinton was considering visiting India for the celebrations, and that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright may visit in September or October.
Shervani will be accompanied by a high-level business delegation, the spokesman said.
The United States is India's largest trading partner, and around 70 percent of the South Asian nation's foreign direct investment originates in the United States.

Earlier this year Washington retained India on its list of nations subject to unilateral trade action for allegedly failing to protect intellectual property rights. India strongly objected to the move.
This month Washington declared itself in "outright opposition" to the deployment of ballistic missiles by India and Pakistan, and said it was working to prevent such a move.
The remark was spurred by a newspaper report that India had moved medium-range missiles near the international border with Pakistan, its archrival and a longtime U.S. ally.
New Delhi denied any missile deployment, but officials said some Prithvi missiles had been stored in Punjab state about 100 km (60 miles) from Pakistan.
India says Washington is turning a blind eye to Pakistan's acquisitions of Chinese missiles, which have been denied by both Islamabad and Beijing.
